title: Inverse limits of finite exact group sequences with p-group kernels

source.place: Tag 0BUA (lemma-structure-decomposition), final proof paragraph: inverse-limit exactness with surjective P transitions, details omitted there; the finite-quotient interpretation of pro-p is the product-topology factorization through a finite coordinate

proof.text: Coordinatewise multiplication, identity and inversion preserve the compatibility equations, since every transition is a homomorphism. Thus $I$ and $C$ are subgroups of their respective products, and $P$ is a subgroup of $I$. The compatibility condition $u_{\mu\lambda}(x_\mu)=x_\lambda$ is closed: its complement is a union of the basic cylinders specifying unequal values of these two finite coordinates. Intersecting these closed conditions over all comparable pairs shows that $I$ is closed in $\prod_\lambda I_\lambda$. The same argument applies to $C$; intersecting additionally the closed coordinate conditions $x_\lambda\in P_\lambda$ shows that $P$ is closed in $\prod_\lambda I_\lambda$ and in $I$. The compatible families with coordinates in $P_\lambda$ are exactly $\varprojlim_\lambda P_\lambda$. Its subspace topology from $I$ agrees with that from $\prod_\lambda P_\lambda$: in both cases basic opens restrict finitely many coordinates to arbitrary subsets of $P_\lambda$.

proof.text: Apply [lem-galois-closed-subgroup-product-finite-groups] to the closed subgroups $I\leq\prod_\lambda I_\lambda$ and $C\leq\prod_\lambda C_\lambda$ from Step 1. Both are profinite topological groups, in particular compact and Hausdorff, with precisely the subspace topologies of the statement.

proof.text: The identity $\theta_\lambda u_{\mu\lambda}=v_{\mu\lambda}\theta_\mu$ says that $(\theta_\lambda(x_\lambda))_\lambda$ is compatible whenever $x\in I$, so it defines $\theta:I\to C$. Multiplication is respected at every coordinate. The inverse image of a basic cylinder in $C$ is a finite intersection of conditions $x_\lambda\in\theta_\lambda^{-1}(U_\lambda)$, open in $I$ because the coordinates are finite discrete. Hence $\theta$ is continuous. Moreover $\theta(x)=1$ if and only if every $x_\lambda\in\ker\theta_\lambda=P_\lambda$. Thus $\ker\theta=P$, and normality follows directly from $\theta(yxy^{-1})=\theta(y)1\theta(y)^{-1}=1$ for $x\in P$, $y\in I$. Closedness of $P$ is already proved in Step 1.

source.place: Tag 0BUA (lemma-structure-decomposition), proof, inverse-limit construction and final paragraph; omitted details supplied explicitly

proof.text: Fix $c=(c_\lambda)_\lambda\in C$ and let $X_\lambda=\{x\in I_\lambda:\theta_\lambda(x)=c_\lambda\}$. Each $X_\lambda$ is finite nonempty by surjectivity of $\theta_\lambda$. Commutativity and compatibility of $c$ make $u_{\mu\lambda}$ restrict to maps $X_\mu\to X_\lambda$, with the inherited identity and composition laws. These restrictions are surjective: given $x\in X_\lambda$, choose $z\in X_\mu$. Then $a=x\,u_{\mu\lambda}(z)^{-1}$ lies in $P_\lambda$, since both factors have image $c_\lambda$. Choose $b\in P_\mu$ with $u_{\mu\lambda}(b)=a$, using the assumed surjectivity on kernels. Now $bz\in X_\mu$ and $u_{\mu\lambda}(bz)=a\,u_{\mu\lambda}(z)=x$. Apply [lem-galois-inverse-limit-surjective] to this inverse system of finite nonempty sets on the given directed index set. A compatible family in $\varprojlim X_\lambda$ is an element $x\in I$ satisfying $\theta(x)=c$. This proves surjectivity of $\theta$.

source.place: Tag 086J (lemma-nonempty-limit), applied to the explicitly constructed surjective system of fibres; fills the exactness details omitted in pione.tex Tag 0BUA

proof.text: Let $q:I\to I/P$ be the coset map. The formula $\bar\theta(q(x))=\theta(x)$ is well-defined because $P=\ker\theta$. It is a homomorphism, surjective by Step 4, and injective because $\theta(x)=\theta(y)$ implies $\theta(x^{-1}y)=1$, hence $x^{-1}y\in P$ and $q(x)=q(y)$. By Step 2 the source $I$ is compact and the target $C$ is Hausdorff; Step 3 gives continuity and Step 4 gives surjectivity. Thus [lem-sfb-compact-hausdorff-surjection-quotient] makes $\theta$ a quotient map. For every subset $W\subseteq C$ we have $q^{-1}(\bar\theta^{-1}(W))=\theta^{-1}(W)$. The definition of the quotient topology for $q$, followed by the open-set criterion for the quotient map $\theta$, gives $\bar\theta^{-1}(W)$ open in $I/P$ if and only if $W$ is open in $C$. Since $\bar\theta$ is bijective, it and its inverse are continuous. This proves the asserted isomorphism of topological groups.

proof.text: The restrictions $u_{\mu\lambda}|_{P_\mu}:P_\mu\to P_\lambda$ form an inverse system of finite nonempty sets: they are homomorphisms, so each group contains its identity, and their surjectivity is an explicit assumption. The identity and composition laws are inherited from $u$. Apply [lem-galois-inverse-limit-surjective] to this system. With the identification of Step 1 this says that each coordinate homomorphism $\pi_\lambda:P\to P_\lambda$ is surjective.

source.place: Tag 086J (lemma-nonempty-limit), projection-surjectivity fibre application as recorded in lem-galois-inverse-limit-surjective

proof.text: Let $f:P\to Q$ be any continuous surjective homomorphism to a finite discrete group. Its kernel $f^{-1}(\{1\})$ is an open neighbourhood of the identity. From the basic neighbourhoods of the product subspace topology in Step 1, there is a finite set $J\subseteq\Lambda$ for which $N_J=\{x\in P:x_j=1\text{ for every }j\in J\}\subseteq\ker f$: refine each of the finitely many coordinate neighbourhoods to the singleton identity in its discrete group. Choose $\lambda$ above every $j\in J$, by repeated pairwise directedness; if $J$ is empty, choose any $\lambda$ using nonemptiness of $\Lambda$. For $x\in\ker\pi_\lambda$ and $j\in J$, compatibility gives $x_j=u_{\lambda j}(x_\lambda)=u_{\lambda j}(1)=1$. Hence $\ker\pi_\lambda\subseteq N_J\subseteq\ker f$.

proof.text: Using surjectivity of $\pi_\lambda$ from Step 6, define $\bar f:P_\lambda\to Q$ by $\bar f(a)=f(x)$ for any $x\in P$ with $x_\lambda=a$. If $x,y$ have the same coordinate, $x^{-1}y\in\ker\pi_\lambda\subseteq\ker f$ by Step 7, so this definition is independent of the lift. Lifts of $a$ and $b$ multiply to a lift of $ab$, proving that $\bar f$ is a homomorphism. Since $f=\bar f\pi_\lambda$ is onto, $\bar f$ is onto. Put $K=\ker\bar f$. Choose a lift $a_q\in P_\lambda$ of each $q\in Q$. The disjoint fibres of $\bar f$ are exactly $a_qK$, and $k\mapsto a_qk$ is a bijection $K\to\bar f^{-1}(q)$ with inverse $a\mapsto a_q^{-1}a$. Counting these finite disjoint fibres gives $|P_\lambda|=|Q|\,|K|$, so $|Q|$ divides the power of $p$ equal to $|P_\lambda|$. Every positive divisor of $p^n$, with $p$ prime, is $p^m$ for some $0\leq m\leq n$: repeatedly remove factors $p$ from the divisor; any remaining factor greater than one would have a prime divisor different from $p$ dividing $p^n$, impossible by primality. Therefore $|Q|$ is a power of $p$, including $|Q|=1=p^0$. This proves the final clause without assuming that the abstract group $P$ is a torsion $p$-group.
